parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man books a pitch at a campsite.
script: Good morning, Oakvale Campsite, Megan speaking.
Hello. I'd like to book a pitch for this summer.
Of course. Could I have your name?
Felix Braun. B, R, A, U, N.
When would you like to arrive?
On the third of June, for four nights.
Will you be in a tent, a caravan or a campervan?
Do you have any preference for the location of the pitch? We have pitches near the river or near the woods.
The river sounds nice, but I've heard it can be noisy with families. I'd prefer somewhere quiet, so near the woods, please.
Would you like an electricity hook-up? It's five pounds extra per night.
So that comes to twenty-eight pounds per night in total.
That's fine. Are there any facilities on site?
There's a small shop that sells basic food, and fresh bread is delivered every morning.
Great. Are there any rules I should know about?
Just one main one. Quiet time starts at ten p.m., and we ask everyone to keep noise down after that.
No problem. What time can we arrive?
Check-in is any time after two p.m.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: An organiser talks about a walking festival.
script: Good evening, everyone. I'm Gareth, and I'm one of the organisers of the Valley Walking Festival. This year is a special one, because it's our twentieth anniversary.
All the guided walks must be booked online in advance. We can't accept people who simply turn up on the day, because numbers on each walk are limited.
There's a shuttle bus between the town and the start of each walk, and it's free for anyone with a festival booking.
As for the weather, we'll walk in rain or wind. Walks are only cancelled if there's an official storm warning.
Let me tell you about some of the walks. The Lakeside Ramble is flat and short, and it's suitable for families with young children.
Eagle Crag involves a steep climb of about four hundred metres, so it's only for fit walkers, but the view from the top is fantastic.
The Island Trail begins with a short boat trip across the lake, and then you explore the island on foot.
The Star Walk is a night walk, led by a local astronomer, so bring a torch and warm clothes.
On the Marsh Hide Walk, the focus is on birds. Our guide is an expert, and binoculars are provided.
And finally, the Ridge Marathon is our longest walk, at twenty-six kilometres. It's a real challenge.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Ella and Josh, discuss their research on community gardens.
script: Ella, let's go through our community gardens project. Why did we choose it again?
Because the council is considering selling some of the land used for community gardens to developers. We wanted to find out what the gardens mean to people.
Right. And we interviewed twenty gardeners at four different sites.
What surprised me was that the main benefit people mentioned wasn't the food. It was the social connections, meeting neighbours and making friends.
Yes. But the main problem everyone mentioned was the waiting lists. Many people wait years for a plot.
I'd suggest creating new gardens on rooftops. There's a lot of unused flat roof space in the city.
Good idea. Let's check the figures. There are thirty-five community gardens in the city.
And the average waiting time for a plot is three years.
The most commonly grown crop is tomatoes, followed by beans.
Forty-five percent of the gardeners we interviewed were over sixty.
And for our proposal, we'll suggest starting with the rooftops of libraries, because the council owns them and many have flat roofs.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on how cities are changing wildlife.
script: Today I want to talk about a surprising idea: that cities are causing animals and plants to evolve, sometimes very quickly.

The classic example is the peppered moth in Britain. During the Industrial Revolution, pollution from coal blackened tree trunks, and dark-coloured moths, which were better camouflaged, became far more common than pale ones. When air quality improved, the pale moths returned.
Many more examples have now been found. Blackbirds in European cities sing at a higher pitch than those in forests, which helps their songs to be heard above the low rumble of traffic.
Urban birds also tend to lay their eggs earlier in the year, perhaps because cities are warmer and food is available for longer.
In Puerto Rico, lizards living in cities have evolved longer legs and stickier toe pads than forest lizards, which help them run and cling to smooth surfaces such as walls and windows.
In the London Underground, there's a form of mosquito that appears to have adapted to life in the tunnels, where it bites humans and rats rather than birds.
Plants are changing too. White clover in many cities produces less cyanide, a chemical that protects it from being eaten, possibly because urban environments have fewer grazing animals.
Behaviour changes as well. Coyotes in Chicago have become active mainly at night, to avoid people.
What's striking is the speed. These changes have happened over decades, not centuries. Many of the studies rely on citizen science, with volunteers recording observations across many cities.
Finally, there are practical lessons. If we want cities to support wildlife, planners should include green corridors that allow animals to move between parks and other habitats.

passages.title: The Invention of Paper
paragraphs: Before paper existed, people wrote on a wide variety of materials. The ancient Egyptians used papyrus, made by pressing together thin strips of a reed that grew along the Nile. In Europe and the Middle East, important documents were written on parchment, which was made from specially prepared animal skin. Both materials worked well, but papyrus could only be produced where the plant grew, and parchment was expensive.

Traditionally, the invention of paper is credited to Cai Lun, an official at the Chinese imperial court, who presented his method to the emperor in 105 AD. He made paper from a mixture of mulberry bark, hemp, old rags and even worn-out fishing nets, which were soaked, beaten into a pulp, spread on a screen and dried. However, archaeologists have found fragments of paper in China that are older than Cai Lun, so it is likely that he improved and standardised an existing process rather than inventing it.

For several centuries, papermaking remained largely a Chinese skill. According to a popular story, the technique reached the Islamic world after the Battle of Talas in 751, when Chinese papermakers were taken prisoner and forced to share their knowledge in Samarkand. Whatever the truth of this story, paper mills were soon established in the Islamic world, including one in Baghdad around 794. Paper helped make Baghdad a great centre of learning.

Papermaking reached Europe through Spain in the twelfth century, and spread to Italy, where the town of Fabriano became famous for its paper in the thirteenth century. Fabriano's papermakers introduced several innovations, including watermarks: faint designs pressed into the paper that identified the maker and are still used today, for example in banknotes.

For most of its history, paper was made from old cloth. As demand grew with the spread of printing, rags became scarce. In the nineteenth century, inventors developed methods for making paper from wood pulp, which made paper cheap and plentiful. However, much of this paper contained acids that caused it to turn yellow and crumble over time, creating a serious problem for libraries, whereas older rag paper often survives in excellent condition.

Despite predictions that computers would create a 'paperless office', the world still uses enormous amounts of paper, particularly for packaging. Recycling has become an important part of the industry, although paper fibres become shorter each time they are recycled, so new fibres are always needed.

passages.title: Saving Seeds for the Future
paragraphs: Over thousands of years, farmers developed a vast range of crop varieties, each adapted to local soils, climates and tastes. During the twentieth century, much of this diversity disappeared, as farmers around the world switched to a small number of high-yielding varieties. According to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization, around three-quarters of the genetic diversity of crops was lost during that century. This matters, because traditional varieties may carry genes for resistance to diseases, pests or drought that future farmers will need.

To protect what remains, countries have established seed banks, which store seeds at low temperatures so that they remain alive for decades or even centuries. The most famous is the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, which opened in 2008 on a remote Norwegian island in the Arctic. Built deep inside a mountain, where the permafrost keeps it naturally cold, it stores seeds at around minus 18 degrees Celsius. It now holds more than 1.2 million samples deposited by seed banks from almost every country.

The vault is often described as a backup for the world's agriculture, and in 2015 it was used for the first time. Because of the civil war in Syria, the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas could no longer operate its seed bank near Aleppo. Researchers withdrew copies of their seeds from Svalbard, planted them in Lebanon and Morocco, and used the new harvest to rebuild their collection.

Other seed banks focus on wild plants rather than crops. The Millennium Seed Bank, run by the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, in England, works with partners around the world to collect and store the seeds of wild species, many of them rare or threatened. Its aim is to bank the seeds of 25 percent of the world's plant species.

Seed banks have limitations, however. Some plants produce what are known as recalcitrant seeds, which die if they are dried and cannot survive freezing. These include important crops such as cocoa and avocado, as well as many tropical trees. For such species, scientists are developing other techniques, such as storing tiny pieces of plant tissue in liquid nitrogen.

Many experts also argue that seed banks should not be the only solution. Seeds stored in a vault do not evolve, while crops grown in farmers' fields continue to adapt to changing conditions. Supporting farmers who grow traditional varieties, alongside storing seeds, may be the best way to protect crop diversity for the future.

passages.title: Should We Stop Tipping?
paragraphs: Tipping, giving extra money to people who provide a service, is so deeply rooted in some countries that it is easy to forget it is a matter of custom rather than necessity. The practice began in Europe, probably in the seventeenth century, when wealthy guests gave small sums to servants in the houses where they stayed. It later spread to restaurants and hotels.

In the United States, tipping became widespread after the Civil War. Many employers, particularly railway companies and restaurants, hired formerly enslaved workers and paid them little or nothing, expecting customers to provide their income through tips. This history continues to shape the system today. Under federal law, employers can pay workers who receive tips a minimum wage of just 2.13 dollars an hour, a figure that has not changed since 1991, as long as tips bring their total earnings up to the normal minimum wage.

Supporters argue that tipping rewards good service and gives workers an incentive to work hard. Yet research suggests that the link between tips and service quality is weak. Studies by the psychologist Michael Lynn have found that the quality of service explains only a small part of the variation in tips. Factors such as the server's appearance, the weather and even whether the server draws a smiley face on the bill can have a larger effect. Some studies have also found that customers tip some groups of workers less than others, which raises concerns about discrimination.

Customers, too, are growing frustrated. In recent years, digital payment screens have begun to suggest tips of 20 percent or more, even for services such as buying a coffee at a counter, where tipping was once uncommon. This phenomenon, sometimes called 'tip creep', has made many people feel pressured to pay more than they intended.

Other countries show that different systems are possible. In Japan, tipping is not expected and may even cause confusion. In much of Europe, restaurant prices include a service charge, and tips, if given, are small. Workers in these systems receive a regular wage that does not depend on the generosity of customers.

In my view, tipping is an unfair way of paying people. It makes workers' incomes unpredictable, shifts responsibility for wages from employers to customers, and allows bias to affect earnings. I believe that service workers should be paid a fair wage by their employers, with prices adjusted accordingly. Including a clear service charge in prices would be more honest for customers and more secure for workers.

task1.text: The table below shows the percentage of the population in three age groups in one country in 1980 and 2020, with a projection for 2050. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The table shows the proportion of the population in one country aged 0 to 14, 15 to 64, and 65 and over in 1980 and 2020, together with projections for 2050.

Overall, the population is ageing significantly. The share of children has fallen and is expected to continue falling, while the proportion of older people has risen sharply and is projected to double again by 2050. The working-age population has remained the largest group throughout.
In 1980, children aged 0 to 14 made up more than a third of the population, at 35%, while people aged 65 and over accounted for just 5%. The working-age group, those aged 15 to 64, represented 60%.

By 2020, the proportion of children had dropped to 22%, while the share of older people had more than doubled to 13%. The working-age population had risen slightly to 65%. By 2050, children are projected to make up only 16% of the population and the working-age group to fall back to 58%. Meanwhile, people aged 65 and over are expected to account for over a quarter of the population, at 26%, which would make them a larger group than children.

task2.text: Some people think it is better to rent a home, while others believe that buying a home is a better choice. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
model: Deciding whether to rent or buy a home is one of the biggest financial choices most people make. While buying is often seen as the safer long-term option, renting has important advantages. In my view, the right choice depends on a person's circumstances, but for most people buying is better in the long term, once they are settled.

Those who prefer renting point to flexibility and lower initial costs. Renters do not need to save a large deposit, and they can move easily if they change jobs or want to live in a different area. This is particularly valuable for young people early in their careers. Tenants are also usually not responsible for major repairs, such as a broken roof or boiler, which can be very expensive for homeowners. In addition, in cities where property prices are extremely high, renting may be the only realistic option.

On the other hand, buying a home offers security and long-term financial benefits. Homeowners cannot be asked to leave by a landlord, and they are free to decorate or modify their homes as they wish. Over time, mortgage payments build ownership of a valuable asset, whereas rent is money that is never recovered. Once the mortgage is paid off, housing costs fall dramatically, which can be very important in retirement.

In my opinion, renting makes sense for young people and those whose jobs or plans may change. However, for people who intend to stay in one place for many years, buying is usually the wiser choice, because it provides stability and a secure financial future.
In conclusion, although renting offers flexibility, I believe that buying a home is generally the better option for people who are ready to settle down.

speaking.cue:
Describe a time you spent in a natural place.
You should say:
- where it was
- when you went there
- what you did
and explain how you felt about the experience.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about a weekend I spent in the tea gardens of Srimangal, in the north-east of Bangladesh, which is sometimes called the tea capital of the country. I went there last winter with two friends, mainly to get away from the noise of Dhaka before our exams. We stayed in a small eco-resort surrounded by hills covered in tea bushes, and on the first morning we woke up early to walk through the plantations while the mist was still lying in the valleys. It was so quiet that all we could hear were birds. Later that day, we visited Lawachara National Park, a rainforest nearby, where a local guide took us along a trail and pointed out hoolock gibbons swinging high up in the trees. I'd never seen apes in the wild before, so that was a real highlight. In the evening, we tried the famous seven-layer tea, which has seven different coloured layers in one glass. What I remember most is how calm I felt the whole time. I hadn't realised how stressed I was until I was surrounded by nature, and I came back to the city feeling completely refreshed.
